latest.headline: Profit fell 18.5% as the new cigarette tax bit, while almost everything that is not cigarettes grew fast.
body: ITC reported its July-September quarter on 2 November 2026. Consolidated profit fell 18.5% to ₹4,229 crore. Net sales (what ITC keeps after passing the excise duty on to the government) rose about 4% to ₹20,269 crore. The operating margin, the share of each rupee of sales left after running costs, dropped to 28% from 34% a year ago.

Ignore the headline revenue jump of about 44%. That is mostly tax: since 1 February 2026 the government collects more GST and excise on every pack, and the money passes through ITC's books on its way to the state. The number that matters is cigarette profit, which fell 27% to ₹3,813 crore, on net cigarette revenue down 21%. ITC says legal industry volumes "remain under pressure" and that seizures of smuggled cigarettes have risen sharply. The one hopeful sign: cigarette profit was about 14% higher than in April-June.

The rest of ITC had a good quarter. FMCG-Others (Aashirvaad, Sunfeast, Bingo and the rest) grew sales 19% and profit 31% on a consolidated basis, its fastest sales growth in 14 quarters. Paper grew 36%, but part of that is bought: ITC completed its ₹3,498 crore purchase of Century Pulp and Paper on 1 August 2026, so paper is no longer comparable with last year (like for like, sales rose 10%). Agri grew 12%. Cigarettes still made about 74% of segment profit, which is why the total went down. There were no big one-offs: ₹25.66 crore of deal expenses for the paper acquisition, and that is it.

What to watch next: October-December is still compared with a quarter from before the tax rise, so expect another weak year-on-year line. The better tell is whether cigarette profit keeps rising from one quarter to the next. Also watch the interim dividend, usually declared with the December-quarter results: first-half profit is down 17%, and last year's ₹14.50 per share already used up 88% of profit.

oneLiner: ITC pays you a 4.9% dividend and earns 29% on equity, yet trades like a problem stock. The problem is simple: cigarettes fund almost everything, and the taxman just took his biggest slice in years.

verdict.keyQuestion: The tax rise has landed and cigarette profit is down by about a quarter. Can price increases win enough of it back to keep the ₹14.50 dividend whole?

overview: ITC sells four things: cigarettes, packaged foods (Aashirvaad atta, Sunfeast biscuits, Bingo chips), farm commodities, and packaging. Strip away the variety and it is really one business wearing four coats. Cigarettes are 41% of sales but about 80% of the profit, and everything else is small beside them. So picture ITC as a machine that turns cigarettes into cash, with a silent partner at the table: the government, which never put in a rupee but takes a larger cut of every packet whenever it likes. That partner is the whole story. In January 2025 ITC sold off its hotels, a business that had tied up a fifth of its money for almost nothing, so what is left is leaner and points at one job: take the cash and hand it to owners.

editorial.realBusiness: ITC turns cigarettes into cash and hands it to owners, while a silent partner (the taxman) keeps raising his cut.
editorial.whyExists: ITC earns its place because it owns something rare: a cigarette business the law protects. Heavy taxes and licensing rules mean no new rival can simply set up shop and undercut it, so ITC keeps 75-78% of the organised market. Bolted to that is a plain fact: roughly ₹16,000 cr of spare cash walks in the door every year with no better home than your pocket. The foods business is smaller today, but it is the option on a future that is not built on smoke.
editorial.whyNotAlreadyWon: Because the same law that protects the moat also caps it. The government is the silent partner, and every few years it raises the rent. February 2026 was the latest reminder: tax on cigarettes jumped from 28% plus a cess to a flat 40%. That ceiling is why even a leader earning 29% on equity will never be handed the rich price a clean compounder gets. You are not really competing with Godfrey Phillips for this business. You are sharing it with the state.

mentalModels.why: High taxes, excise duties and brand licensing create a barrier no new entrant can cross. The cigarette market is oligopolistic and ITC is the 75-78% leader.
29% ROE and 39% ROCE are high. Debt/Equity is 0.034, near zero, with interest coverage of 329x.
Free cash of ₹16,332 cr in FY26. Profits turn to cash immediately because cigarettes are all cash business.
80% of operating income from cigarettes means any tax increase directly hurts. Feb 2026 proved this is not theoretical: cigarette segment profit fell 27% in Jul-Sep 2026.

FMCG-Others is India's number two listed packaged-foods business but only 27% of revenue and ~11% EBITDA margins versus 30%+ for the core. Rerating depends on scale and margin expansion, neither assured.
The tobacco business carries an ethical overhang. Institutional investors avoid it. That is why the multiple is compressed relative to the cash and returns.

economicEngine.label: Volume
economicEngine.value: Cigarette sticks sold, plus FMCG products sold
economicEngine.note: Cigarette volumes squeeze when taxes rise; FMCG volumes grow low-mid single digits.

economicEngine.label: Price
economicEngine.value: Retail price per stick, per unit of FMCG
economicEngine.note: Cigarettes get price increases to offset taxes; FMCG pricing is set by competition, chiefly HUL and Nestle.

economicEngine.label: Margin
economicEngine.value: Profit per stick, after all taxes, couplings, distribution
economicEngine.note: Cigarette margin is taxed at ~65-75% of retail price. Any tax raise directly squeezes the per-stick profit.

economicEngine.label: Capital
economicEngine.value: Cash, not capex; the business requires minimal reinvestment
economicEngine.note: Capex is low and declining (₹2,321 cr in FY26 is mostly for FMCG/agri expansion, not cigarette capacity).

economicEngine.label: Returns
economicEngine.value: Free cash returned to shareholders via dividend and buyback
economicEngine.note: The entire economic point is taking cash out, not reinvesting it.

strategicPosition.label: Smaller cigarette rivals
strategicPosition.description: Godfrey Phillips (10%), VST (9%). Lower scale, lower margins, no diversification.

strategicPosition.label: ITC
strategicPosition.description: 75-78% of organised cigarette market, number two in listed packaged foods, near-zero debt, 4.9% dividend yield, paying cash.

strategicPosition.label: HUL, Nestlé, Britannia
strategicPosition.description: Dominant in FMCG, higher margins, consumer trust. If ITC FMCG ever reaches parity scale with them, the rerating is real. Not there yet.

winningToday: ITC is the clear cigarette leader, generating 80% of operating profit from a moat that is wide and protected.
Near debt-free, 29% ROE, 39% ROCE, and throwing off ₹16,000+ cr of free cash annually.
Dividend yield of 4.9% on a ₹295 stock, with FY26 payout ₹14.50 per share, is legitimately high.
Hotels demerger (completed January 2025) freed up capital that was earning 3-4% returns and now redeploys into cigarettes and FMCG.
FMCG-Others is quietly expanding margins (11% EBITDA, up from 9-10% a few years ago) and is India's number two listed packaged-foods play.
stopWinning: Cigarette volume declines when taxes rise. Feb 2026's GST bump to 40% is already doing it: ITC says legal industry volumes remain under pressure and seizures of smuggled cigarettes have risen sharply.
80% of operating income from a single, ever-taxed product is a fundamental ceiling on the business's ability to re-rate.
FMCG margins (11% EBITDA) are still a third of HUL/Nestle, and gaining share against those giants is slow and capital-intensive.
The ESG overhang is real and not going away. Institutional investors screen out tobacco on principle, capping the multiple permanently.
At 19.7x earnings that are still shrinking and 5.2x book, there is no obvious margin of safety if taxes rise again or FMCG disappoints.
marketBets: Cigarette tax regime stabilises. February 2026 was a shock; the next one is not priced in.
FMCG-Others can keep expanding to 15-20% of profit, but this requires years of scale and margin gains.
The ₹14.50 dividend (about 4.9% yield) holds even while FY27 earnings shrink.
The market is willing to keep ITC at a 3-4x discount to a pure FMCG multiple because of the tobacco anchor.
No major activist or M&A. ITC stays as is, returning its cash to owners.

sectorModels.reading: Single-digit or negative in cigarettes, low-mid double-digit in FMCG
sectorModels.note: Cigarette volumes are under pressure from taxes and ESG. FMCG volume growth is real but competed fiercely.
Cigarette gross margin is cushioned by pricing power but compressed by taxes. FMCG margin is driven by mix and scale.

sectorModels.reading: ITC has nationwide distribution and brand reach rivalling HUL
sectorModels.note: The cigarette network (retail touchpoints, distribution) is one of India's best and doubles as the FMCG backbone.

sectorModels.reading: Cigarettes have it, via tax pass-through, though at some volume cost. FMCG does not (HUL, Nestle, Britannia price-set).
sectorModels.note: The tension: ITC is a price-taker in FMCG but a price-maker in cigarettes (because of taxes). Over time, FMCG will be the business; pricing power is at risk.
No other FMCG business is as tax-exposed. This is ITC's singular tail risk and the reason the multiple is perpetually capped.

editorial.whyNow: Why is the price where it is? Because the market sold first and the accounts caught up later. The stock is down about 28% over the past year, and the February 2026 tax jump to 40% has now shown up in two straight quarters of falling profit. Results day itself barely moved the price (about ₹266). It has since climbed to ₹295 as of 18 November, still in the lower half of its ₹253-411 range. Two things make this a cleaner moment to judge ITC than a year ago. The hotels are gone (the demerger finished on 29 January 2025), so a low-return hotel chain no longer blurs the picture. And the tax shock is now a number in the accounts rather than a guess. If you can stomach cigarette risk and you are honest that this is a 5% a year holding (the dividend plus whatever pricing claws back), the debt-free balance sheet and the 88% cash conversion are still doing real work for you.
editorial.remember: ITC pays you about 5% a year to wait for a smoke-free future that may never fully arrive. Take the cheque, but do not mistake it for growth.

business.unitOfRevenue: A cigarette stick sold or a unit of FMCG (atta, biscuit, snack). For ITC, the unit economics are split: cigarettes throw off high-margin cash; FMCG is a lower-margin business scaling gradually.
business.revenueModel: Selling cigarettes through a national network of 50+ lakh retail points, commanding 75-78% of the organised market. Selling FMCG brands (Aashirvaad, Sunfeast, Bingo, Yippee, Classmate, Vivel) through the same distribution and competing head-to-head with HUL, Nestle, Britannia and Dabur. Selling agri-products and packaging to B2B customers.

segments.name: Cigarettes
segments.marginProfile: Operating profit margin 30%+; the absolute cash cow. Volumes under pressure from taxes and ESG.

segments.name: FMCG-Others
segments.marginProfile: EBITDA margin 11%, slowly expanding. Revenue ₹24,210 cr, +10.1% YoY. Profit ₹1,803 cr +14% YoY shows margin leverage. Still dwarfed by HUL (25%+ EBITDA margins) but is India's number two listed packaged foods play.

segments.name: Agri-Business
segments.marginProfile: Lower margin, volumes-driven. Procurement and trading model keeps margins thin but stable.

segments.name: Paperboards, Paper, Packaging
segments.marginProfile: Commodity-like, thin margins, serves both internal (cigarettes, FMCG) and external demand.

business.revenuePerUnitTrend: Cigarette sticks per capita and per distribution point are flat to declining as taxes and ESG reduce volume. Retail price per stick rises yearly to offset taxes but volumes shrink. FMCG revenue per unit is growing modestly as brand mix shifts upward and pricing power improves. The blended picture is low-single-digit volume growth masking cigarette volume declines.

industry.structure: Cigarettes are a government-protected oligopoly. ITC (75-78%), Godfrey Phillips (10%), VST (9%), others (2-3%). FMCG is a competitive, scale-driven market with HUL as the clear leader (30%+ of packaged foods), followed by Nestle, Britannia, Dabur, ITC and others. FMCG is fragmented and consolidating.
industry.competitors: Cigarettes: Godfrey Phillips, VST. FMCG: HUL, Nestle, Britannia, Dabur. ITC competes as a distant number two in packaged foods, with one advantage rivals lack: the cigarette cash flow funds FMCG growth.
industry.pricingPower: In cigarettes, ITC has strong pricing power and raises prices to pass on tax increases, though pushed too far that costs volume and invites down-trading. In FMCG, pricing power is weak to moderate (HUL and Nestle price-set). Blended, pricing power is moderate.
industry.demandDriver: Cigarettes are driven by addiction, habit and ritual (sticks consumed per smoker per day). FMCG is driven by income growth, urbanisation and household consumption. Agri is driven by food processing and export demand.
industry.driverType: Cigarettes are recession-resistant but tax-sensitive. FMCG is counter-cyclical to HUL/Nestle (ITC takes share in downturns). Agri is cyclical.
industry.tam: Cigarette TAM in India is ~₹90,000-1,00,000 cr annually (organised). FMCG is far larger, ₹10,00,000+ cr. ITC's share of each is constrained by competition and cigarette regulation.
industry.penetration: Cigarettes: 75-78% organised market (high). FMCG: <2% of total packaged foods market. Room to grow but not easily.
industry.valueChainPosition: Manufacturer selling directly to retail through distribution. No captive distribution; depends on the strength of the distribution network and brand trust.

business.qualityVerdict: Is it well run? Yes, and the numbers are not shy about it: 29% on equity, 39% on capital, no net debt, a dividend near 5%. The cigarette business is real, profitable, and hard to kill. The foods business is competent but walks straight into HUL and Nestle and grows slower than they do. Put it together and ITC is a high-quality, low-growth machine that turns almost all of its profit into cash. The quality was never the question. The question is the ceiling the taxman keeps lowering.

valuation.label: Stock P/E
valuation.hint: check: 295 / 15.08 = 19.6; up from 17.6 mostly because EPS fell 9%

valuation.label: P/B
valuation.hint: moderate; ROE 29% justifies a premium, ESG discount explains it is not higher

cashFlowNote: Operating cash flow is steady and clean (₹18,464 cr in FY26), and roughly matches reported profit, which is what funds the dividend. Capex is modest (₹2,321 cr, 2.9% of revenue), mostly for FMCG and agri-capex, not cigarette capacity (which requires almost no reinvestment). Free cash was ₹16,332 cr in FY26. The ₹14.50 dividend costs roughly ₹18,200 cr in total (about 1,254 cr shares), so it is funded by operating cash flow (₹18,464 cr) with any balance drawn from ITC's large cash pile (₹38,128 cr), not by borrowing. The cash is real and tracks profit.

ratios.label: ROE
ratios.hint: 3Y avg 35.2% (includes demerger gain in FY25), but 29% is still elite

ratios.label: Debt/Equity
ratios.hint: nearly debt-free; ₹491 cr borrowings at Sep 2026 (₹2,399 cr in March), ₹30,135 cr investments

ratios.label: Operating Margin
ratios.hint: 28% in Q2 FY27 vs 34% a year ago; the tax hit shows here

ratios.label: FMCG-Others EBITDA Margin
ratios.hint: FY26; 10.4% in Q2 FY27 (standalone); vs HUL 25%+, room to grow

growth.label: Sales TTM
growth.hint: Q2 FY27 +4% after Q1 -11%; the tax change muddies comparisons

growth.label: Profit CAGR 5Y
growth.hint: but driven by FY25 demerger gain

growth.label: Profit CAGR 3Y
growth.hint: underlying (ex-demerger) growth is ~6%, held back by taxes and FMCG margin lag

growth.label: Profit TTM
growth.hint: Q1 FY27 -16%, Q2 -18.5% as the new cigarette tax bites

growth.label: Stock CAGR 10Y
growth.hint: almost flat; the multiple has been range-bound

growth.label: Stock CAGR 5Y
growth.hint: modest, mostly from dividend, not price appreciation

growth.label: Stock CAGR 3Y
growth.hint: has underperformed while profit grew; multiple compressed on tax and ESG fears

management: Professionally managed, no promoter (ITC is a rarity: 0% promoter holding, run by independent board and management). DII 49.81%, FII 33.22%, Retail 16.93%. The lack of promoter overhang is a genuine positive, removing single-family risk. Management has executed the hotels demerger cleanly, completed 29 January 2025, unlocking ₹38,128 cr of on-balance-sheet investments. The demerger rationale was sound: hotels used 20% of capital for 3-4% profit. Now that capital can redeploy to cigarettes (high-return, cash-harvesting) and FMCG (lower returns today but scale optionality). On 1 August 2026 it closed the ₹3,498 cr purchase of Century Pulp and Paper from Aditya Birla Real Estate, a bet on paperboard rather than on cigarettes or foods. This is competent, transparent capital allocation.

sources: Cigarette regulatory moat: high taxes, excise duties, brand licensing create barriers to entry. 75-78% of organised market.
Distribution network: 50+ lakh retail points, unmatched density in cigarettes and dual-use for FMCG.
Brand and consumer habit: ITC cigarettes (Gold Flake, Classic) are iconic, driving repeat purchase and pricing power.
Vertical scale: owns production, distribution, retail relationships across both cigarettes and FMCG, allowing cross-subsidies and cost arbitrage.
moat.note: The moat is real and wide, and it is the reason ITC prints cash. But it is a moat with a landlord. Regulation and brand protect the cigarette margin, and the very same regulation lets the government take more of it whenever the budget needs money (February 2026 proved the point again). In foods, ITC has the reach but no price premium over HUL or Nestle, so the moat there is barely dug. Here is the hard irony: the cigarette moat is what pays the dividend, and also what keeps the price down, because the state pockets much of the upside.

narrative: The last two years are a story of one clean-up and one shock. The clean-up: in January 2025 ITC spun off its hotels as a separate company (keeping a 40% stake), a business that had swallowed a fifth of the company's capital while earning just 3-4%. Freeing that money was the right call. The shock came in February 2026, when the government moved cigarette tax from 28% plus cess to a flat 40% and squeezed the profit on every stick almost overnight. By mid-2026 that shock had reached the accounts: consolidated profit fell 16% in April-June and 18.5% in July-September, almost all of it from cigarettes. Look past cigarettes and the business is fine. FY26 revenue was ₹78,868 cr, up about 5% on a FY25 figure that was puffed up by a ₹17,803 cr one-time gain from the demerger, and underlying profit grew roughly 6%. The foods arm (Aashirvaad, Sunfeast, Bingo) grew revenue about 10% and profit 14% in FY26, and sped up to 19% sales growth in July-September, but it is still small and thinner-margin. So the engine works. It is just that the biggest cylinder still runs on cigarettes, and the taxman still decides how much fuel it gets.
risks: Tax escalation. The February 2026 GST bump to 40% has landed: cigarette segment profit fell 27% year on year in July-September. The next tax change (whenever it comes) will hurt again. High severity because cigarettes are 80% of profit.

Volume decline. Higher taxes + ESG screening = lower volumes. Down-trading (premium to budget cigarettes) and illicit trade compress industry volumes. ITC loses volume alongside the industry. ITC itself now flags a sharp rise in seizures of smuggled cigarettes. Medium to High severity.

FMCG margin trap. FMCG-Others is growing revenue and profit, but margins (11% EBITDA) are still a third of HUL/Nestle. Gaining share in a mature market is capital-intensive and may not expand margins. Medium severity.

ESG screening. Many institutional investors, especially global funds, screen out tobacco by mandate. This shrinks the investor base and keeps the multiple compressed. The discount has persisted for years with no sign of reversing. Medium severity.

Dividend pressure. FY26's ₹14.50 per share already took 88% of profit, and first-half FY27 profit is down 17% (₹8,738 cr against ₹10,530 cr). If the second half looks like the first, a flat ₹14.50 would cost more than the whole year's profit, and the gap would come out of the cash pile. ITC can afford that for a while. It cannot do it forever. Medium severity.
Interest rate shift. If rates stay high or rise further, the roughly 5% yield becomes less attractive. ITC could see outflow as investors chase higher rates elsewhere. Low to Medium severity.

FMCG underperformance. If ITC FMCG fails to scale or loses share to HUL/Nestle, the profit mix never shifts away from cigarettes and the re-rating never comes. Low to Medium severity (execution dependent).

trapChecklist.label: Earnings backed by cash
trapChecklist.note: Free cash ₹16,332 cr in FY26, and operating cash flow tracks profit at ~88%.

trapChecklist.label: Earnings growth
trapChecklist.note: H1 FY27 profit down 17% on the cigarette tax. Non-cigarette profit grew, but not enough to offset it.

trapChecklist.label: Balance sheet strength
trapChecklist.note: Debt/Equity about 0.01 (₹491 cr borrowings at Sep 2026), investments ₹30,135 cr. Near-zero debt.

trapChecklist.label: Dividend sustainability
trapChecklist.note: FY26 dividend ₹14.50/share is about ₹18,200 cr total, roughly 87% of profit, covered by operating cash flow (₹18,464 cr) and a touch above free cash flow (₹16,332 cr). With FY27 profit falling, the cover is getting thin.

trapChecklist.label: Valuation multiple ceiling
trapChecklist.note: 19.7x on shrinking earnings already reflects a meaningful tax and ESG discount; a sustained re-rating would need tax stability or a material shift in the profit mix.

trapChecklist.label: One-time gains masking trend
trapChecklist.note: FY25 net profit (35,052 cr) included ₹17,803 cr hotels demerger gain. Underlying profit was ~17,249 cr, so FY26 was -22% YoY. This is disclosed but easy to miss.

sectorChecklist.label: Volume growth
sectorChecklist.note: Cigarette volumes under pressure from taxes (Feb 2026 GST raise); net cigarette revenue fell 21% in Q2 FY27. FMCG volumes growing but slower than market.

sectorChecklist.label: Gross margin
sectorChecklist.note: Cigarettes ~60% gross, FMCG ~40%. Blended margin healthy but cigarette margin tax-squeezed every 2-3 years.

sectorChecklist.label: A&P and distribution
sectorChecklist.note: ITC has the best cigarette distribution (50+ lakh points) and co-uses it for FMCG. Clear advantage.

sectorChecklist.label: Pricing power
sectorChecklist.note: Cigarettes have unusually strong pricing power, but tax pass-through can come at the cost of volume and down-trading. FMCG does not (HUL/Nestle price-set). Blended pricing power is moderate and declining as FMCG grows.

sectorChecklist.label: Tax and regulatory stability
sectorChecklist.note: Cigarette taxes are a permanent headwind. Feb 2026 proved it. No relief expected. This is the core sector risk for ITC.

summary: ITC is a cash-rich, high-quality business that sells cigarettes (about 80% of profit) and a smaller, growing foods arm. It earns 29% on equity, carries almost no debt, throws off ₹16,332 cr of free cash a year, and pays you about 4.9% to hold it. At ₹295 and 19.7x earnings that are still shrinking, the price is fair for an income holding and stingy about anything more. The whole tension fits in one line: the cigarette moat is real and profitable, but the taxman caps it, and foods is too small to lift the ceiling yet. If you want a 5-6% return and can sit still through the odd tax shock, ITC does that job. If you want growth, look elsewhere.

engine.earnings: Before February 2026, ITC grew earnings in the low single digits because two forces cancelled out: cigarettes losing a little volume every year, foods growing off a small base. Blended, that was 6-7% underlying profit growth. This year the engine is running backwards. The tax rise took a big bite out of profit per stick, and foods, even growing sales 19% and profit 31% in the latest quarter (the numbers are in the note at the top), earns too little to fill the hole. What restarts the engine is cigarette pricing catching up with the tax without pushing smokers to smuggled packs. The early sign is modest: cigarette profit rose from April-June to July-September. Past that, the old ceiling still applies. Nothing makes this engine race unless taxes settle down or foods becomes a far bigger share of profit, which is a decade's work if it happens at all.
engine.multiple: The P/E went from 17.6x in August to 19.7x now, and almost none of that is excitement. The price rose about 6% while trailing earnings per share fell from ₹16.51 to ₹15.08. When earnings shrink, any stock looks dearer at the same price. If October-December looks like July-September, expect a bit more of that. The trailing year still includes four months from before the new tax (October 2025 to January 2026), and only when every month in it carries the new tax will the P/E describe the post-tax business. Underneath, the market is still stapling a tax-and-conscience discount to the stock. Few investors will pay 22-25x for a business that could lose 15-20% of its profit in a single budget. It just did. What would un-cheap it is dull: years of tax calm, or foods growing big enough to change what ITC even is.
engine.verdict: So here is my honest read. The earnings engine has stalled for a year, and the market marked the stock down before the damage showed up in the accounts, so there is no cheap surprise waiting to be found. You are buying a roughly 5% cheque and the patience to keep holding it. That is a fine thing to own if you know that is what it is. It is a miserable thing to own if you were secretly hoping for a growth stock in disguise. Best case, cigarette pricing catches up and you compound quietly on the dividend. Worst case, profit keeps sliding and the cheque gets trimmed. I lean towards the dull, steady outcome. I would change my mind if cigarette profit starts falling from one quarter to the next again, or, in the good direction, the day foods finally outgrows the smoke.

lenses.name: The tax ceiling
lenses.reading: ITC's whole moat sits on the government's cigarette tax, and that same tax is a slow-ticking clock. Every few years the rate climbs, the stock drops on the shock, then steadies as ITC quietly passes the tax on to smokers. Do that enough times and the shareholder is really the one absorbing a heavier bill each cycle. February 2026 was the steep version of that rhythm, not the gentle one, and the July-September accounts show what steep costs: this time ITC chose not to pass it all on, because pricing up fully would have pushed smokers to smuggled packs. A long pause from here would be a gift. Neither is yours to control, which is exactly the point.

lenses.name: What FMCG has to become
lenses.reading: The right question is not whether the foods business is good. It is how big it has to get before it changes ITC's price. Today it earns about ₹1,800 cr, roughly 7% of the company's operating profit, against cigarettes at about 80%. For foods to become even a quarter of the profit, it would need to roughly triple or quadruple toward ₹6,000-7,000 cr, growing sales and pushing margins from about 11% up toward the mid-teens. At its FY26 pace of ~14% profit growth, that is the better part of a decade away. The mix is already shifting a little, but for the wrong reason: cigarettes fell to about 74% of segment profit in July-September mostly because cigarette profit shrank, not because foods took over. So treat foods as a real but slow option on a higher price, not the reason you own the stock this year. It is not nothing. It is just not soon.

lenses.name: The ESG discount
lenses.reading: A chunk of ITC's discount has nothing to do with cash and everything to do with conscience. Many global funds are barred by their own rules from owning tobacco at any price. That quietly shrinks the pool of buyers: ITC is held mostly by domestic institutions (about 50%) and retail (about 17%), while foreign funds have been trimming, down about 4 points to 33% over the past year. Put a precise number on the discount and you are guessing, so I will not pretend to. The point is that it is real, it has lasted years, and it is a permanent drag on any smoke-to-foods re-rating rather than a passing mood.

lenses.name: Bond-like income, equity risks
lenses.reading: People buy ITC the way they buy a bond: for the roughly 5% cheque, which took about 87% of FY26 profit and was covered by the cash coming in. But it is not a bond, and forgetting that is the trap. A bond's coupon does not shrink when the government changes a tax. ITC's profit just did, and the payout left little slack to absorb it. Treat bond-like as a description of the income, not a promise about safety. Could it double in five years? Only with 20%+ earnings growth or a huge re-rating, and neither looks likely. The realistic deal is plain: collect 5% while the price treads water, and call that a fair return. What you are buying is stability and a cheque, not capital gains.
